entries.title: About the Course
entries.content:
Each year in high school, students read one of the gospels along with several other New Testament epistles. For 2026-2027, they read the gospel of Luke along with Romans, Ephesians, Hebrews, and Revelation. Using their study Bibles and other resources, students encounter scripture and seek to understand the cultural, historical, and theological context of their readings in order to more deeply appreciate the richness of the Bible and the humility needed in order to live out God's word today.

This topic is included in the following course(s): Bible: Grade 12

entries.title: Placement & Combining Tips
entries.content: Lessons in one of the gospels are shared across HS grades. Some epistles studied in Grade 12 are more challenging than those in younger grades, but lessons can be combined if desired. Students new to reading the Bible for themselves or unused to commentaries or study notes may find the lessons in Grades 7-8 a gentler introduction to these study practices.

blocks.text: Take a moment to recall what you read previously in the same book or topic.

Read the passage assigned or read for the number of minutes allocated. If a book is challenging for you, try stopping to narrate to yourself silently now and then to make sure you are tracking. Or you could listen to an audiobook version of the text and read along. You may also want to read aloud to yourself. If a book is an easy read, enjoy the ride! Keep an eye out for quotes to put in your Commonplace Book or events or characters to put down in your Book of Centuries.

Process and integrate your reading by narrating either orally or in writing. Some lesson plans will give you a suggestion of how best to narrate. You might want to set a timer to keep yourself on track, so you stop reading with enough time to narrate.

Read notes in your Study Bible or commentary. Look up places mentioned in the text in your Bible atlas. Add something to your Book of Centuries or Commonplace Book. Jot down additional reflections and thoughts in your Bible notebook or share with others.

Read over the lesson plans to familiarize yourself with the content for accountability and interest. If doing the lessons together, use a picture, a map, or an engaging question to rouse students' interest before reading. You may also highlight one or two unfamiliar terms if needed. If in a classroom context, you may choose to leave larger doctrinal conversations for students to have with their parents at home.

lessons.title: 30m New Testament: Grade 12 - Lesson 1
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, Luke for Everyone, Introducing the NT

➜ INTRO
Each year, we read one of the Gospels along with our study of the rest of the New Testament books. This year, we will be reading Luke along with Romans, Ephesians, Hebrews, and Revelation. It is helpful to be continually reminded of who Jesus is and how he interacted with people. The Gospel accounts (and all the rest!) were designed to be read many times. There will be insights gained that you would only pick up after multiple readings and by paying attention to repeated words and themes. 

We will make use of the Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes and maps, Introducing the New Testament (selections), a Luke commentary (selections), and some Bible Project videos to help us understand what Luke and the other authors are saying to their audiences. Then we can think about what new thoughts about God we gain in the process. You do not need to read all the study notes for all the verses. Pick and choose based on which verses you have questions about. Use a digital or physical notebook to record your thoughts as you work your way through the readings. 

➜ VIEW & NARRATE
Today and over the next few weeks, we will set the stage for reading Luke and the other books by gaining some context. Narrate silently in your head or by talking to yourself to go over the main points. Write down a few of them in your journal. If you followed the Alveary 11th-grade plans last year, you may be familiar with this video. The review will be helpful as you will notice new things this time through.
∞ Video Link: How to Read the New Testament

➜ READ & NARRATE
Introducing the New Testament
Ch.1 p.17-24
Make a list with a short description of the rulers in Palestine at the time of Jesus.
 
➜ MAP WORK
When places are named in the text, refer to a map in the study Bible. Finding the places on the map is very helpful for seeing the stories in the context of the land. Sketching your own maps of journeys or regions can be helpful too.

lessons.title: 30m New Testament: Grade 12 - Lesson 2
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, Luke for Everyone, Introducing the NT

➜ READ  
Luke 1

➜ NARRATE & RESPOND
Talk over to yourself what you just read. Then, respond to what you read by putting down a few of your thoughts or questions. Just as in nature study, when we ask questions such as, “What do I notice? What do I wonder? What does this remind me of?” we can ask the same questions about what we read.

➜ READ 
Pick one of the Luke for Everyone readings discussing verses from Luke 1. Jot down any new insights or thoughts. 

➜ READ 
Introducing the New Testament
Ch.1 p.31-32 "Social Systems" - "more than they needed."
Write a paragraph summarizing the mindset of the NT world towards wealth and poverty.
lessons.teacherNotes:
★ STUDENT/TEACHER NOTE
Instead of reading Luke for some of the lessons, consider watching and listening to Luke via the LUMO Project, which only uses the actual text of Luke but has people acting while it is read. There are many versions and many languages available. You might consider this resource for your modern language studies, too. However, be sure to ask yourself, "What did the film add visually that the Gospel text itself did not explicitly say?” as any visualization project requires interpretive decisions to be made.

∞ Video Links: 
Lumo Project Luke 1:1-38
Lumo Project Luke 1:39-80

terms.content: · • NT: What is Luke's emphasis in his gospel? What new thoughts did this reading provide about who Jesus is? What other insights did you gain?

· • NT: What is the overall structure and message of Romans? What new thoughts did this reading provide? What other insights did you gain?

· • NT: Tell the main themes in Ephesians. What new thoughts did this reading provide? What other insights did you gain?

· • NT: What are the main themes of Hebrews? What new thoughts did this reading provide? What other insights did you gain?

· • NT: What is the structure of Revelation, and what are the main themes? What new thoughts did this reading provide? What other insights did you gain?
